_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section rather than repeating its words, and each has a near-miss in another section. Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 1.
title: Starting again
subtitle: Four people describe what happened when they changed career.

sections.A: Priya, former accountant, now a furniture maker. For nine years I worked as an accountant for a large firm in Leeds, and I was good at it. But I'd always made things in my spare time, shelves, a table for my sister, and gradually the weekends became the part of the week I actually cared about. I didn't tell anyone at work what I was planning. I just spent two years taking evening classes in carpentry while still doing my day job, which was exhausting. People imagine that making furniture is relaxing, and in a way it is, but I hadn't realised how much it would take out of me physically. Some days I can hardly lift a cup of tea by the evening. The money is unpredictable, of course, but I'd saved for that. What I didn't expect was how much I'd miss the people. Accounting is surprisingly social; a workshop is not.
sections.B: Daniel, former airline pilot, now a primary school teacher. Flying was all I'd wanted to do since I was a boy, so leaving it surprised everyone, including me. After my daughter was born I hated being away for days at a time, and I started volunteering at a reading club at her school on my days off. Within a year I'd applied for teacher training. I earn about a third of what I used to, and we've had to give up a lot: the bigger house, the holidays abroad. I don't mind. Oddly, the classroom isn't as different from the cockpit as you'd think. Pilots are trained to stay calm when things go wrong and to follow a clear routine, and both of those turn out to be very useful with a class of thirty seven-year-olds. Some of my former colleagues think I've wasted my training, but I'd say I use it every day.
sections.C: Ruth, former journalist, now a beekeeper. I was a newspaper journalist for almost twenty-five years, and for most of that time I loved it. Towards the end, though, I felt I was always racing a deadline that someone else had set. I'd kept a few beehives as a hobby, and when the paper offered voluntary redundancy, I took it. My son, who'd always found my job rather boring, thought the bees were the most exciting thing I'd ever done, and honestly that gave me the confidence to go ahead. Now I sell honey and run courses for beginners. I decide when I work and when I stop, which after a lifetime of deadlines feels like a luxury. If I'm honest, my only real regret is that I waited so long. I could have done this ten years ago and been just as happy.
sections.D: Kenji, former footballer, now a physiotherapist. I'd been a professional footballer since I was eighteen, and I assumed I'd play until my mid-thirties. Then I damaged my knee in a match at twenty-six, and after two operations the surgeon told me it was over. I didn't choose to leave; the decision was made for me. I'd spent so much time with physiotherapists while I was recovering that retraining as one seemed the obvious step, and the studying itself wasn't too difficult. What I wasn't prepared for was how lost I'd feel. For the whole of that first year, I'd see a match on television and have to switch it off. It's better now. Helping someone else get back on their feet after an injury means a lot to me, probably because I know exactly what it's like.

questions.question: Which person had a change of career forced on them by circumstances?
questions.why: 'I didn't choose to leave; the decision was made for me.' Ruth's redundancy was voluntary.

questions.question: Which person has found the new job more physically demanding than expected?
questions.why: 'I hadn't realised how much it would take out of me physically.'

questions.question: Which person says abilities from the previous job are still useful?
questions.why: Staying calm and following a routine 'turn out to be very useful'; 'I use it every day'.

questions.question: Which person accepted a large fall in income?
questions.why: 'I earn about a third of what I used to.' Priya's money is unpredictable, not clearly lower.

questions.question: Which person was given confidence by a relative's reaction?
questions.why: Her son thought the bees exciting, which 'gave me the confidence to go ahead'.

questions.question: Which person wishes they had made the change sooner?
questions.why: 'My only real regret is that I waited so long.'

questions.question: Which person did not share their plans with colleagues?
questions.why: 'I didn't tell anyone at work what I was planning.'

questions.question: Which person trained for the new career while still in the old one?
questions.why: Evening classes in carpentry 'while still doing my day job'. Kenji retrained after he had stopped playing.

questions.question: Which person values having more control over their working hours?
questions.why: 'I decide when I work and when I stop… feels like a luxury.'

questions.question: Which person found the first period after the change emotionally difficult?
questions.why: 'What I wasn't prepared for was how lost I'd feel' for 'the whole of that first year'.
